description:
For two years now, the GeForce RTX 2080 Ti has been the undisputed consumer-level GPU king - but Nvidia's new Ampere architecture has arrived, with RTX 3080 taking performance to the next level. In this review you'll get to see just how fast this new card is, and whether it lives up to the early promise shown in our RTX 3080 early look video. NOTE: we re-tested Gears 5 after filming this - its jump from 2080 to 3080 it actually 69%, not 61%.

Thanks to Omen for sponsoring our channel. Watch Omen Underground Presents Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 1+2 Tournament from the PAX Arena here: https://bit.ly/2ZYE0eH

See all of our performance benchmarks for RTX 3080 in our Eurogamer review: https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/digitalfoundry-2020-nvidia-geforce-rtx-3080-review

comments.text: @Digital Foundry: Great Video thanks. I do have one point of critisism though: You have been heavily pushing the narrative in this video that the 3080 is the next gen variant of the 2080 / 1080. This is a claim that I find wrong. In Ampere,  the biggest GPU (102 chip) is now used in the 3080-Card, in contrast the 1080 and the 2080 cards only contained the 2. largest chip of the generation (104-chips), the product stack has been essentially moved down one level.  I view this as a marketing ploy by Nvidia to enalbe them to claim exorbitant generational leaps. A more honest approach would be to compare the generationally best chip to best chip (102 to 102), second best chip to second best chip (104 to 104) etc.  This would have been a more apples to apples comparison. And in this spirit, it would have been more appropriate to include the 1080-Ti as a point of reference of comparison, rather than the 1080.

comments.text: A lot of people don't understand this 1.9x perf/watt claim.  Like you said, it comes to a power efficiency curve (like power supplies). If you look at the chart, the 1.9x the performance is this: 4k at 60fps the Turing card uses 240W of power to deliver the same 60 frames that the Ampere card gives at 120W (the top end of Turing spectrum vs Ampere).  The higher the performance profile, the lower the efficiency (but Ampere still producing more performance for the same power levels up to Turing's max).  And I also think the power requirement has to do with Samsung vs TSMC choice NVidia made.

@rebootcomputa  they are correct tho. Up until 1080p everything was named after the vertical pixel count (so the 1080 in 1920x1080). Also, I'll be able to make much better use of my LG B9 55" OLED (got on sell for $999.99 on Black Friday normally like $1700.00!)  w/ 2.1 HDMI for G-SYNC, VRR, 4K/120hz, etc.

I may get a PS5 for exclusives but don't see a compelling reason to get an XBOX Series "X" or "S" seeing as the games are available across platforms and I'll be able to play XBOX Series "X" games at much higher graphical and performance (frame rates) settings with my PC equipped with a RTX 3080 / 3090. The only thing I'm a little concerned about is my CPU an I7-8700K@4.8GHZ 6 cores / 12 trends being a "bottleneck" but I'm pretty sure it will still be more than adequate by in large until I decide its time to build a PC from scratch again. Yeah the consoles have 8 cores / 16 trends BUT they only clock to like 3.7 to 3.8GHZ which is yes a HUGE improvement over last generation but still a far cry from enthusiast level CPU performance. After all, there's only so much "magic" that can be done with a $500.00 budget. 

As far as RAM is concerned, I think my 16GB of DDR4@ 3600MHZ should be adequate for quite some time. comments.text:
I guess my opinion will be unpopular here but in for a penny....

I have been looking at building my first PC in about 18 years but I can't quite get to the point where I think it is worth it.

The 3080 looks to be the first card that makes ballpark 4k 60fps possible on almost every game but the investment to get there is pretty huge. After you have got the machine and the card, you've put in £1500-ish and you still need a monitor and this where my issue comes in. If you want anything above 60hz you are looking at £800 - and given PC gamers are generally saying 4k is a waste and that frame rates matter more - a sentiment I agree with by the way I start to wonder what's the point?

Surely then the money is better funneled into a 1440p or 1080p machine which would give the higher frames at a far lower cost.

Worse still if you are limited to 60hz and so reduce the overall benefit of higher FPS then you could buy a PS5 and an Xbox Series X and still have a bucket of cash left over (told you thiis wouldn't be popular)

I have no doubt the tech is great and I love the idea of building a beastly PC but in the end I feel like it really doesn't provide much benefit for anyone who isn't looking to go out and blast £2500+ on their gaming.

Happy to hear converse opinions and be convinced otherwise though.

Happy gaming all :)

You'll find that 90% of these games are demanding or taxing to some degree and they choose them in order to put the hardware under stress (CPU/GPU heavy, RAM heavy ect.). However, by doing it this way, it's also kinda skewing with actual average performance levels that a normal person will experience, as they are only testing how well it'll perform, on demanding games. Back in reality, most people don't just play on demanding games, they'll also play on average AAA titles, graphically weak games, Indie games, multiplayer games, F2P games, MMO's, from old games to new ect. ect. A true, down to Earth test, would instead to test performance using a host of games, just like these, that most normal people actually play on a regular basis and not just on a few selected, highly demanding titles.

comments.text: @stacksmalacks8826  exactly, more frames being pushed means less time for the GPU to get a new frame to the display. So even if you run a 60hz monitor for example but you're running 300fps, the GPU can send a new frame to the display sooner than it can at, say, 200fps. All of the inputs and physics calculations are still being processed at those internal speeds even though the monitor is only updating 60 times per second, but it will receive the newest possible frame the GPU has. This will decrease input latency and improve perceived responsiveness. That's why a higher frame rate is always better even if your monitor can't display all of the frames being rendered.

@UAGoWSuplexer  It is down to a simple thing in gaming: Almost all current games are terrible at utilizing more cores, and we don't know if game devs will change things. Intel currently has fewer cores but higher clocks in the high end, and is strictly worse everywhere else.

Most if not all games have something called a 'world thread', which works better the higher your clocks are.

The 10700k is a powerhouse for core clocks, but is worse on the core amount front.

Meaning:

If you buy low end, get AMD.

If you buy mid end, get AMD.

If you buy high end for a machine that *only* plays games and maybe runs dome word and photoshop, strongly consider Intel.

If you also want to stream with that machine, you need cores again. Then AMD will once again be better.

Power consumption is only a problem in very specific circumstances, most people with that kind of money can afford to acquiesce to the power consumption's downsides. If the 3060 has the same issue, that's when it might be a problem. If they do go for the same brute force power for even the 3060, hopefully they rebrand or just keep selling older RTX 20 series, because with the right pricing, they can be the best way for next gen console parity for PC gamers on a budget and for the masses.

Imagine an RTX 2060 or rebrand (or even cut down Ampere, although I wonder about the power consumption) for like a much reduced $150-$200 price, that would get you entry level RTX, fully DLSS compatible, DX12 Ultimate support, and RTX IO, basically gearing you up for next gen games that will be fully utilizing those features. This is probably the best way to get a lot of people to get next gen console parity without spending that much. 

(Yes, I know the RTX 2060 is probably not as powerful as the Xbox Series X, but it's a hell of a lot better than a GTX 1080 Ti, which will fall behind terribly due to not supporting all those features.
